intro: A radial basis kernel turns squared distance into a smooth similarity. Its bandwidth controls how rapidly a neighbor stops looking similar.
task: Return the pairwise Gaussian radial-basis kernel matrix between two sets of feature rows.
requirements: first is an (n,d) matrix and second is an (m,d) matrix. gamma is a scalar in [0,1e6].
Return a matrix K with K[i,j]=exp(-gamma*sum((first[i]-second[j])**2)). Use squared Euclidean distance.
gamma zero returns all ones. Equal rows have similarity one; no normalization by the number of features or by row sums is applied.

Use real finite numeric inputs with magnitude at most 1e6, excluding booleans. Vectors have length 1..128 and matrix axes have length 1..128 unless a tighter bound is stated. Leave all inputs unchanged; raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

examples.name: Zero gamma
Squared distance

hints.title: Find the structure
hints.body: Expand one sample axis from each matrix to obtain all pairwise coordinate differences.

hints.title: Build the calculation
hints.body: Sum squared differences along the feature axis before applying the negative exponential; do not normalize kernel rows.

explanation: The exponential maps zero distance to one and large distance toward zero. Multiplying squared distance by gamma sets the length scale of that decay.
A kernel matrix is not an attention probability matrix: its rows need not sum to one. Keeping cross-set shape explicit makes the same operation usable for training and evaluation rows.
